summary: This informational memo is a guide to finding useful information on the Internet, as a way to improve on how hard it was to locate resources then. The author describes techniques to make useful sources easier to reach, with the goal of hiding the route to them.

plainLanguage.summary: This memo is a map of the Internet's information resources as they were in 1993: which lists existed, where the file archives were, who to ask for help, and how to look up a person or a program. It shows how people found things before there was a web to search.

questions: how to find information on the internet in 1993
subtitle: A 1993 guide to finding the information that was on the network, and the services that would help you find it.

tldr.problem: By 1993 there was so much material on the network that finding the useful part was itself a problem, and the routes to it were impossible to hold in your head.
tldr.mechanism: The memo is a catalogue of lists, indexes, libraries, archives, information centers and lookup tools, with the exact commands for reaching each one, and it explains how Archie searches the anonymous FTP archives for you.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1402 is an Informational FYI memo from January 1993 that obsoleted RFC 1290. It has not been obsoleted since.

today: RFC 1402 is an Informational FYI memo published in January 1993 that obsoleted RFC 1290. It has not been obsoleted since, and it records the Internet's information resources and the commands for reaching them as they were in 1992.

sections.title: Why a Guide to Finding Information
sections.content:
The memo is a list of the essential things, in the author's view, that people responsible for providing network information should have as reference material. One of the basic problems with information is making it easily available to those who need the data. Libraries have performed a cataloging function for many centuries, but information flow is now provided so fast that it is difficult to keep up with it, even partially, and computer networks have only added to the problem by opening up access to even more information.

Making that wealth of information available poses three problems. First, people need to know of its existence, and the memo provides an index to the network's information, where most of the documents listed are pointers to the final information. Second, even when you know a document exists, you may not know whether it is important or relevant, because few of us are knowledgeable in more than a limited area; this is where librarians help, being familiar with the research databases that individuals search in law, mathematics and many other fields. Third, once existence and importance are known, the information has to be indexed so that researchers can find it, which the author calls the most difficult task of the three. Information on the network is rarely static: it is always moving, growing, changing and dying, and computers should be able to help manage that ever-changing environment, but for now the information has to be catalogued as it passes by.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo frames the problem in three parts: knowing a resource exists, knowing whether it is worth reading, and being able to find it again later. It mainly helps with the first.

sections.title: Getting Access to the Internet
sections.content:
A frequently asked question in 1993 concerned how the average person got access to the Internet. The most common way was electronic mail, which made it possible to communicate with anyone on the Internet and on other networks, with many gateways between them. For example, using CompuServe, a large commercial electronic information and communication service, mail could be sent to and from individuals on the Internet.

A direct connection provided capabilities that mail could not. One was the ability to establish a connection to a remote computer from your own computer, which is what the program Telnet does. Many universities and large research companies had Internet connections and paid considerable fees for them, and if you were associated with one you might already have access or be able to get it. Another was the ability to transfer a file from a remote computer, which is what FTP, the file transfer protocol, does.

For people without a direct connection, the memo reproduces a frequently asked question posting listing the ways in: an account on a public access bulletin board system connected to the Internet, or an account with a network service provider offering a dial-in service. It gives the costs at the time, from $40 to $100 a month for part-time dial-up shared between customers, through $250 a month for a dedicated 9600 bps line, to $4,000 a month for a dedicated T1 at 1.44 Mbit/s, with one-time startup fees of $100 to $8,000. It then lists the known service providers with the speeds and services each offered.
sections.plainLanguage: Mail was the usual way in. A direct connection added Telnet for logging into remote machines and FTP for fetching files, and the memo lists the dial-up providers and what they charged in 1993.

sections.title: Lists, Indexes and Bibliographies
sections.content:
Section 2 is the index itself, listing documents that point at other resources. The Internet Resource Guide is an index of major resources available on the network, with chapters on computational resources, library catalogs, archives, white pages, networks, network information centers and miscellaneous; it could be fetched by anonymous FTP from NNSC.NSF.NET or searched by keyword over Telnet at pac.carl.org, the Colorado Alliance of Research Libraries.

A separate document lists all the sites on the Internet that support anonymous FTP, and could be searched through Archie. The index of all RFCs points at a set of older documents, including RFC 1118, the Hitchhiker's Guide to the Internet, RFC 1175, a bibliography of internetworking information, and RFC 1208, a networking glossary of terms.

Further entries cover a list of existing mailing lists and groups, the responsible use policies of the regional networks, and campus ethics and policy statements. Later sections cover the libraries available over the network, the anonymous FTP sites themselves, the network information centers, network statistics including monthly figures for NSFNET backbone traffic by packets and bytes, campuswide information systems, bulletin board systems and interactive databases, and WHOIS for finding people. The memo ends with a short list of books and a selection of free periodicals, including PC Week, MacWEEK, Info World and Network World.
sections.plainLanguage: The bulk of the memo is an index: documents that point at documents, arranged by what you are looking for. Each entry gives the exact commands to fetch or search the resource it describes.

sections.title: Anonymous FTP and Archie
sections.content:
Throughout the document, sites are listed for specific documents, and most are only indexes to more information. The memo says that a big problem is searching through all of this information to find what you want, and that one of the best search methods is Archie.

Archie, the Archive Server Listing Service, is the tool for finding a program available through anonymous FTP. Several Archie servers were scattered around the world. Archie goes to every site that offers anonymous FTP files, collects the file structure from that site, and places it in a database it can search. The memo walks through a worked example: reading an article about Windows that mentioned a shareware program called ZiPaper, whose file was named zipapr.zip, and then telnetting to archie.ans.net, logging in as archie and typing prog zipapr.zip. The reply names the host, the last update time, the location and the file itself, which tells the reader that the file is available by anonymous FTP to that host in that directory.

The glossary defines anonymous FTP as the ability to transfer a file from a remote computer connected to the Internet without having an account on it: connect with FTP, give userid anonymous, give your e-mail address as the password, use dir to list files, cd to change directory, get to fetch a file, binary before get for a binary file, and quit to end the session. The largest repository described is the Mirrors directory at Washington University, which holds a copy of all the wsmr-simtel20.army.mil files, with separate subdirectories for MS-DOS and Macintosh material; the memo warns that the site is often overloaded and difficult to connect to.
sections.plainLanguage: Anonymous FTP let anyone fetch a file without an account. Archie was the search engine for those archives: it kept a listing of what was on each server so that you could search by keyword instead of browsing.

sections.title: WHOIS and Finding an Address
sections.content:
WHOIS is a program on many computers that connects to another computer and, given a person's name, responds with the information it holds about that person. A similar program called finger does the same kind of thing, except it only supplies information about individuals who have an account on that specific computer, whereas a WHOIS database generally holds information about most of the individuals at a university rather than just those on the machine you connect to.

In a larger sense, the memo says, WHOIS is a technique for finding a person's e-mail address. There is no master list of e-mail addresses on the network, and standards for supplying them have been established but will take some time to be globally implemented; in the meantime the easiest way to find out is to call and ask.

The resources listed include a document compiled at Carnegie-Mellon University with an alphabetical listing of universities and the searching techniques unique to each, a program called Netfind that queries the network in an organized way to find e-mail addresses, and the Inter-Network Guide, which gives the addressing needed to reach someone on a different network, such as addressing a CompuServe message as 12345.1234@compuserve.com where the numbers are the person's CompuServe ID. The memo also lists the universities running a WHOIS service and a short list of WHOIS servers.
sections.plainLanguage: WHOIS was the way to find a person: you queried a database for a name and got back contact details. The memo notes that there was still no master list of e-mail addresses, and recommends a telephone call when the stakes are high.

sections.title: A Glossary of the Terms Used
sections.content:
The glossary explains the terms the memo uses. BITNET is a network of mainframes or minicomputers that connects many universities and colleges and provides e-mail and file transfer, but not remote login. The Internet is a very large network that connects just about any types of computers and supports e-mail, file transfer and remote login. Anonymous FTP is the ability to transfer a file from a remote computer connected to the Internet without having an account on it. Telnet is the ability to establish a connection to a remote computer, using either a program that gives a VT100-type terminal emulation or TN3270 for a full-screen IBM 3270-type connection. Listserv is a program available on many BITNET-connected computers that acts as a mail forwarding system and as a file repository, and it is also how you subscribe to a mailing list.

After the glossary, the memo closes with a short security note: security issues are not discussed in this memo. It also says that the information was assembled from multiple sources acquired from the network, much of it from reading newsgroups and trying things out, and that it was as accurate as the author had been able to determine as of July 17, 1992, using a DEC 5500 system running Ultrix to check most of the sources.
sections.plainLanguage: The glossary defines the terms the memo uses, and the closing note says the information was checked in mid-1992 and that the memo does not discuss security.
